claims.text: High-temperature HEAs can develop and retain a self-limiting protective oxide layer.
The diffusion of key protective elements such as Al or Cr is slower than the inward diffusion of oxygen.
Slower diffusion of protective elements relative to oxygen causes those elements to oxidize preferentially.
Preferential oxidation of the protective elements produces a compact, adherent, and stable oxide scale.
A compact protective oxide scale blocks further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
An HEA containing sufficient Al and/or Cr can potentially develop an adherent protective scale.
Changing only the concentration of protective oxide-forming elements provides a controlled comparison for testing the hypothesis.
Continuous dense Al2O3, Cr2O3, or composite oxide layers can impede both oxygen ingress and metal-cation egress.
Thermodynamic stability causes the selected protective elements to oxidize preferentially.
The balance between oxygen and protective-element diffusion rates governs both development and retention of the protective layer.
Increasing the concentration of protective elements will significantly lower oxidation mass gain relative to the low-content baseline.
Increasing the concentration of protective elements will produce a thinner, more uniform, and more continuous oxide scale.
A baseline deficient in protective oxide-forming elements will form less-adherent or porous scales and oxidize more rapidly.
Mn-rich oxides can be non-protective and deplete an HEA of Mn.
The proposed differential-diffusion mechanism applies in oxidizing environments at approximately 900–1100 °C.
The mechanism may fail in aggressive atmospheres or at much lower temperatures.
Complex multielement chemistry and microstructure can affect oxide-scale structure, adherence, and growth in HEAs.
The hypothesis would be falsified if the enhanced-element variant has statistically indistinguishable or poorer mass gain, scale thickness, and scale quality than the baseline.
